version.headline: Spacing out study sessions beats cramming
version.summary: A review of hundreds of experiments found that people remember material much better when the same study time is split into sessions spread over days, rather than packed into one sitting.
version.deeper_explanation: Cepeda and colleagues pooled results from 317 experiments reported in 184 articles. Distributed practice improved later recall compared with massed practice, and the best gap between sessions grew with how long the material needed to be remembered.
version.limitations: Most of the studies used verbal material such as word lists and facts; the benefit for complex skills is less well measured.

version.headline: Testing yourself helps you remember more than rereading
version.summary: Students who practised recalling a passage remembered more of it a week later than students who spent the same time rereading it, even though rereading felt more effective.
version.deeper_explanation: In Roediger and Karpicke's experiments, rereading did slightly better on a test five minutes later, but practising retrieval did clearly better on tests two days and one week later. The testing effect has since been replicated many times, in labs and in classrooms.
version.limitations: Over very short gaps rereading can look better; the advantage of testing shows up after a delay.

version.headline: 'Willpower runs out like a battery' failed a large replication
version.summary: A famous idea held that using self-control drains a limited resource. When 23 labs repeated a standard ego-depletion experiment with a shared, preregistered method, they found an effect close to zero.
version.deeper_explanation: The original ego-depletion studies from the late 1990s were cited thousands of times and inspired popular advice about willpower. The 2016 multilab project, with 2,141 participants, found an effect size of about d = 0.04, with a confidence interval that included zero.
version.limitations: This tested one experimental task. Supporters argued other tasks might still show the effect, so the debate continued.

version.headline: A second big test of ego depletion found at most a tiny effect
version.summary: In 2021 a team that included researchers who had supported ego depletion ran a new preregistered test across 36 labs. The effect they found was very small, close to zero.
version.deeper_explanation: This study was designed with input from supporters of the theory to answer the criticism of the 2016 replication. With more than 3,500 participants, it estimated an effect of about d = 0.06, far smaller than the original studies suggested.
version.limitations: It tested specific lab tasks. It does not rule out mental fatigue in everyday life, but it makes a large lab effect very unlikely.

version.headline: We ignore how common things are when judging what's likely
version.summary: Kahneman and Tversky showed that when people read a vivid description of someone, they judge the person's job by how well the description fits a stereotype, largely ignoring how common each job actually is.
version.deeper_explanation: Participants were told how many engineers and lawyers were in a group, then given a short personality sketch. Their judgements barely changed when the proportions changed. This tendency is now called base-rate neglect.
version.limitations: How strong the effect is depends a lot on how the problem is worded; presenting the numbers as counts of people reduces it.

version.headline: '10 out of 1,000 people' is easier to reason about than '1%'
version.summary: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage found that people solved test-result problems correctly far more often when the numbers were given as natural frequencies (counts of people) instead of probabilities and percentages.
version.deeper_explanation: Without any training, correct answers rose from about 16% with probability formats to about 46% with frequency formats. The approach has since been widely recommended for explaining screening results to patients and doctors.
version.limitations: Frequency formats help a lot but do not make everyone reason correctly; many people still get these problems wrong.

version.headline: Sleep helps turn new memories into lasting ones
version.summary: A major review concluded that sleep after learning supports memory consolidation: activity in the sleeping brain appears to replay and strengthen recently learned information.
version.deeper_explanation: Diekelmann and Born reviewed evidence that slow-wave sleep supports memories for facts and events, partly through the reactivation of new memories involving the hippocampus, while REM sleep may matter more for some other kinds of memory.
version.limitations: Much of the evidence on mechanisms comes from animal studies and lab tasks; how much one night's sleep changes everyday learning varies.

version.headline: Did bringing back wolves change Yellowstone?
version.summary: After wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995–96, some researchers reported that less browsing by elk let aspen and willow regrow along streams: a 'trophic cascade' running from predators down to plants.
version.deeper_explanation: Ripple and Beschta reviewed the first 15 years after reintroduction and argued that wolves, by reducing elk numbers and changing where elk feed, let young trees recover in places. Other ecologists dispute how large and widespread the effect is, pointing to bears, cougars, human hunting, drought and beavers.
version.limitations: Recovery has been patchy, and later studies argue the popular 'wolves changed the rivers' story is too simple.

version.headline: Your body keeps blood sugar steady with a negative feedback loop
version.summary: When blood glucose rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps cells take up glucose. As glucose falls, insulin release drops. The response pushes against the change: that is negative feedback.
version.deeper_explanation: When glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which signals the liver to release stored glucose. Two hormones working in opposite directions keep levels in a narrow range. In type 1 diabetes the body makes little or no insulin, so the loop breaks.

version.headline: Bank runs can be self-fulfilling
version.summary: Diamond and Dybvig's model showed that a healthy bank can fail if enough depositors expect others to withdraw: each withdrawal makes the next one more sensible. Deposit insurance can remove the reason to run.
version.deeper_explanation: Banks turn short-term deposits into long-term loans. That is useful, but it means a bank cannot repay everyone at once. In the model, if depositors fear a run, running becomes the best choice for each of them. Diamond and Dybvig shared the 2022 economics Nobel prize with Ben Bernanke for research on banks and financial crises.
version.limitations: It is a mathematical model, not a measurement; real runs also depend on actual losses, rumours and policy.

version.headline: Separate what you control from what you don't
version.summary: The Enchiridion opens by dividing things into those within our power (our judgements, intentions and desires) and those that are not (our body, property and reputation). Epictetus argues that much distress comes from treating the second kind as if it were the first.
version.deeper_explanation: Epictetus, a former slave who taught in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, did not write the book himself: his student Arrian recorded his teachings. This 'dichotomy of control' became one of the best-known ideas in Stoic philosophy.

version.headline: Natural selection needs only three ingredients
version.summary: Darwin argued that if individuals vary, if some of that variation is inherited, and if more are born than can survive, then traits that help survival and reproduction will become more common over generations.
version.deeper_explanation: On the Origin of Species gathered decades of evidence from animal breeding, geology and the distribution of species. Darwin did not know how inheritance worked; genetics later supplied that piece, and natural selection became a foundation of modern biology.

version.headline: Splitting work into small tasks multiplies output
version.summary: Adam Smith described a pin workshop where ten workers, each doing one or two steps, made upwards of 48,000 pins a day, while one person working alone might not make even twenty.
version.deeper_explanation: Smith gave three reasons: workers become more skilful at one task, they lose no time switching between tasks, and specialisation encourages the invention of machines. Later in the same book he warned that very repetitive work could dull workers' minds.
version.limitations: Smith's numbers were an illustration, probably drawn from published descriptions of pin-making rather than his own measurements.

version.headline: Science doesn't only grow step by step; sometimes it changes frames
version.summary: Thomas Kuhn argued that most science works inside an accepted framework, a 'paradigm'. When unexplained anomalies pile up, a field can go through a revolution that replaces the framework, as when sun-centred astronomy replaced the earth-centred system.
version.deeper_explanation: Kuhn called everyday research within a paradigm 'normal science'. His book made 'paradigm shift' an everyday phrase. Critics argued that his account made theory change sound less rational than it is, and Kuhn spent later years clarifying what he meant.

version.headline: Two modes of thinking: fast and slow
version.summary: Daniel Kahneman popularised the idea of 'System 1' (fast, automatic, intuitive thinking) and 'System 2' (slow, effortful reasoning), and used it to explain many systematic errors in judgement.
version.deeper_explanation: Kahneman described the two systems as useful characters rather than literal parts of the brain. The book draws on decades of his work with Amos Tversky on heuristics and biases, for which Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel prize in economics.
version.limitations: Kahneman later acknowledged that he relied too much on some small priming studies cited in one chapter, several of which have not replicated.

version.headline: Learning and thinking need each other
version.summary: In the Analects, Confucius says that learning without thinking is wasted, and thinking without learning is dangerous. Taking in knowledge and reflecting on it are presented as two halves of one practice.
version.deeper_explanation: The Analects is a collection of sayings and short conversations compiled by Confucius's followers after his death in 479 BCE. James Legge's 1861 translation renders this passage: 'Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.'

version.headline: Many everyday English phrases come from the 1611 King James Bible
version.summary: Expressions such as 'the salt of the earth', 'a law unto themselves' and 'the powers that be' entered common English through the King James translation of 1611, which was read aloud in English churches for centuries.
version.deeper_explanation: Linguist David Crystal counted about 257 idioms in modern English that come from, or were popularised by, the King James Bible. Many were first coined by earlier translators such as William Tyndale, whose wording the 1611 translators often kept.
version.limitations: This card is about the history of the English language. Shirori does not present religious texts as advice or proof.

version.headline: 2024 physics Nobel honours the foundations of machine learning
version.summary: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for discoveries that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks, built using tools from physics.
version.deeper_explanation: Hopfield created a network that can store and reconstruct patterns, described with ideas from the physics of magnetic materials. Hinton built on it with the Boltzmann machine, which can learn to recognise characteristic features in data. Their work underpins much of today's deep learning.

version.headline: 2024 chemistry Nobel: designing proteins and predicting their shapes
version.summary: David Baker won half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for computational protein design; Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the other half for AlphaFold2, an AI model that predicts protein structures.
version.deeper_explanation: A protein's function depends on its 3D shape, which used to take years of lab work to determine. AlphaFold2 can predict the structure of virtually all of the roughly 200 million proteins researchers have identified. Baker's group designs entirely new proteins that do not exist in nature.

version.headline: 2024 medicine Nobel for discovering microRNA
version.summary: Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering microRNA, tiny RNA molecules that help control which genes are active in cells.
version.deeper_explanation: They made the discovery while studying a tiny worm, C. elegans. MicroRNAs turned out to exist across plants and animals; the human genome codes for more than a thousand of them.

version.headline: AlphaFold predicted protein structures close to lab accuracy
version.summary: In 2021, DeepMind researchers reported that AlphaFold could predict the 3D structure of many proteins with accuracy competitive with experimental methods, as shown in the CASP14 blind assessment.
version.deeper_explanation: In CASP14, predictions are compared with structures that were solved in the lab but not yet published. AlphaFold's results were far better than other methods for most targets. Its predictions have since been made freely available in a public database.
version.limitations: Accuracy is lower for some proteins, such as those without a fixed shape, and a predicted structure doesn't show how a protein moves or interacts inside a cell.

version.headline: The rule of 72: a quick way to estimate doubling time
version.summary: Divide 72 by a yearly growth rate in percent to estimate how many years it takes for something to double. At 6% a year, money doubles in about 12 years.
version.deeper_explanation: Doubling time is ln(2) / ln(1 + r), which for small rates is close to 69.3 divided by the rate in percent. 72 is used instead because it divides easily and fits common rates of 6–10% well. Its earliest known appearance is in Luca Pacioli's Summa de arithmetica of 1494.
version.limitations: It is an approximation and becomes less accurate at very high growth rates.

version.headline: Look at what's missing: survivorship bias
version.summary: In the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald analysed damage on aircraft that came back from missions. His key point: planes that didn't return are missing from the data, so places where survivors show few hits may be the most dangerous places to be hit.
version.deeper_explanation: Wald developed methods to estimate vulnerability from the damage on surviving planes. The same trap appears whenever we study only successes, such as successful companies or people who 'made it', and forget the failures we can't see.
version.limitations: The popular version of the story, with the widely shared diagram of a plane covered in red dots, is a simplified modern retelling; Wald's actual reports were mathematical.

version.headline: Cognitive behavioural therapy has strong evidence for many problems
version.summary: A review of 269 meta-analyses found the strongest support for CBT in anxiety disorders, somatoform disorders, bulimia, anger control problems and general stress.
version.deeper_explanation: CBT helps people notice and test the thoughts that shape their emotions and behaviour, alongside practical behaviour changes. The review also noted gaps: fewer high-quality comparisons with other active treatments, and limited evidence for some groups, such as people on low incomes.
version.limitations: Strong average results don't mean CBT works for every person, and comparisons with other therapies often show smaller differences.

version.headline: The sky is blue because air scatters short wavelengths more
version.summary: Sunlight contains all colours. Molecules in the air scatter shorter wavelengths, like blue, much more strongly than longer ones, like red, so blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky.
version.deeper_explanation: Lord Rayleigh showed in 1871 that this scattering grows sharply as wavelength gets shorter, roughly with the inverse fourth power. Violet is scattered even more, but sunlight contains less violet and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset light passes through more air, so more blue is scattered away and reds remain.

connection.bridge_sentence: Insulin keeps blood sugar steady by pushing back against change, while a bank run feeds on itself: the difference between negative and positive feedback.

version.headline: The same loop, opposite sign
version.summary: Your body uses negative feedback to pull blood sugar back to normal. A bank run is positive feedback: each withdrawal makes the next one more likely. Same loop structure, opposite effect.
version.deeper_explanation: Engineers, biologists and economists all use the same language of feedback loops. Spotting whether a loop damps or amplifies change tells you whether a system tends to stay stable or run away.

connection.bridge_sentence: The base-rate neglect Kahneman and Tversky found in puzzles shrinks a lot when the same numbers are written as counts of people, which is why natural frequencies are recommended for explaining medical test results.

version.headline: The fix for a famous thinking error is a change of format
version.summary: Psychologists showed that people neglect how common things are. Research on medical risk found that rewriting percentages as counts of people makes the same mistake much rarer.

connection.bridge_sentence: Research on spaced study and research on sleep point in a similar direction: what happens between study sessions, including sleep, matters for what you remember.

version.headline: Memory is shaped in the gaps
version.summary: Psychology finds that spacing out study beats cramming; neuroscience finds that sleep after learning helps stabilise memories. Both suggest the time between learning sessions does real work.

connection.bridge_sentence: Adam Smith's 'division of labour' crossed into biology: zoologist Henri Milne-Edwards wrote of a 'physiological division of labour' between organs, and Darwin used the idea in On the Origin of Species.

version.headline: Darwin borrowed an idea from economics
version.summary: The idea that specialised parts make a whole more productive started in economics with Adam Smith's pin workshop and was carried into biology to explain specialised organs and organisms.

connection.bridge_sentence: Albert Ellis, a founder of cognitive therapy, often quoted Epictetus's idea that people are disturbed not by things but by their views of them, an idea at the heart of CBT.

version.headline: A 2,000-year-old idea inside modern therapy
version.summary: Stoic philosophy taught that our judgements, not events themselves, shape how we feel. Cognitive therapies turned a version of that idea into a structured, tested treatment.
